# How to Improve Your Salon Rebooking Rate?

19 Oct 2026

![How to Improve Your Salon Rebooking Rate?](https://d2mad3kkxvcl7w.cloudfront.net/shrivra_blog_images/blog_1792393301_cf5f38c1.png)

Most salon owners can quote last month’s new-client number from memory. Ask for the rebooking number and there’s usually a pause. We’d argue it’s the one that matters more.

Winning a client isn’t cheap. Between ads, booking-app commissions and the welcome discount, a first visit rarely makes much on its own (it’s the third and fourth visits where things add up). Your salon rebooking rate tells you whether clients get that far.

In the UAE, where people have plenty of choice and many residents move on after a few years, nobody stays loyal by default. Luckily, rebooking responds well to fairly ordinary changes in how you treat clients, follow up and take bookings.

## What Does a Salon Rebooking Rate Entail?

Before attempting to increase it, you need to agree on what the figure means and how to measure it.

### How to Calculate Your Salon Rebooking Rate

Take the number of clients leaving with another appointment fixed, divide by the total number of clients served and multiply by 100.

Rebooking rate = (number of clients who rebooked before leaving ÷ total clients served) × 100

For example, if 180 out of 400 clients rebooked, your rate is 45%. Some salons also count bookings made a day or two later. That’s fine, just stick to one rule.

### What Is a Good Rebooking Rate for a Salon?

Published industry benchmarks put the average somewhere between 40% and 55%, plenty of owners work towards 60%, and the strongest salons pass 70%. A nail bar will rebook more easily than a bridal studio, so compare like with like.

### Why Does Your Salon Rebooking Rate Matter?

Booked appointments are revenue you can plan rotas around. More importantly, I think, a falling rate warns you something has slipped, well before your sales do.

## Why Do Salon Clients Fail to Rebook?

Hardly anyone leaves a salon dramatically. They drift, for reasons that seem too small to matter.

### Weak Follow-up Post-Appointment

Client pays, and that’s often where all contact ends before the promo comes through weeks down the line. Out of sight, out of mind.

### Varied Client Experiences

Where one appointment was fantastic and the most recent was rushed, the client doesn’t know which one they will receive and that alone can drive them away.

### Hard Time Making Appointments

Given that scheduling involves making calls during work hours (with a possible wait on hold), a number of clients will simply decide not to make the effort.

### Lack of Specific Recommendations

They weren’t told how or when they should return, and so their next appointment was optional and things like that don’t happen.

### Forgetting to Book the Next Appointment

Probably the most common one. The client means to book, says they’ll message, gets busy, and suddenly it’s three months later.

## 8 Effective Ways to Improve Your Salon Rebooking Rate

None of these are expensive. If you only try two, start at the top.

### 1\. Encourage Clients to Rebook Before They Leave

Ask at the chair while the client is still happy with the mirror, not at the till as they reach for their keys. “Your colour will need a top-up in about six weeks, shall I put you in for the 14th?” sounds like advice, not a pitch.

### 2\. Recommend the Right Appointment Interval

Most clients have no idea when their fade or gel set needs attention. Tell them. Roughly:

*   Gel or acrylic nails: every 2 to 3 weeks
*   Fades and short men’s cuts: every 3 to 4 weeks
*   Root colour: every 4 to 6 weeks
*   Facials: about once a month

### 3\. Make the Client Feel Special

Think about small things like what colour scheme he or she likes, who their favourite stylist is, and any allergies customers may have stated previously. Clients love it when you remember all these things for them.

### 4\. Send Appointment Reminders in Time

This step doesn’t require daily reminders but at least a single one a couple of days before, provided that the customer is able to confirm or change the appointment without calling.

### 5\. Contact Clients Who Didn’t Rebook

If your client has not yet booked again, contact them a few days before their appointment slot and inquire about their intentions. “Are you ready for another hair trim?” would work better than discounts.

### 6\. Loyalty Points and Privileges

Membership and points systems will work well, allowing loyal customers to choose the Thursday evenings first. The more often, the better.

### 7\. Make Online Booking Simple and Convenient

A lot of booking decisions happen late at night, long after the front desk has gone home. If they can [book online in a few taps](https://salonist.io/features/onlinebooking), you get the appointment. If not, someone else might.

### 8\. Deliver Consistent Service Quality

This one holds the rest up. No reminder can fix a service that changes from stylist to stylist, so set clear standards and train everyone to them.

## How to Use Client Data to Increase Salon Rebooking

Most of what you need is already sitting in your booking history, if you know where to look.

### Track Booking History and Visit Frequency

Compare how often each client comes in with how often you recommended. The gap is where your time should go.

### Identify Clients Who Are Less Likely to Return

These groups are worth flagging:

*   Regulars who are now overdue
*   First-time clients who never came back
*   Anyone who cancelled and didn’t rebook

### Tailor Offers Based on Client’s Preferences

For a client that always books a blow-dry session on Thursday evenings, an offer on spa services will be useless. An offer on booking the first Thursday slot will work, however.

### Track Rebooking Rates of Individual Stylists and Services Separately

Separate the rates for individual stylists and services. A stylist whose rate is way below those of others should be trained on how to conduct the checkout discussion, not on his or her skills.

## The Importance of Reminders and Follow-ups in Rebooking Clients

Timing is just as important as wording. Even a great message sent at the wrong time is doomed to fail.

### Send SMS and WhatsApp Rebooking Messages

In the UAE, WhatsApp is where a lot of clients read their messages, so use it alongside SMS. Salonist’s guide on how to confirm, remind and rebook clients on WhatsApp walks through the setup.

### Create Follow-Up Campaigns for Inactive Clients

Send a friendly check-in once someone is overdue, then one more

# How to Increase Salon Rebooking Rate (From 33% to 58%)

Tips [Mia Chen](https://lutily.com/blog/author/mia-chen) • 7 min read • February 7, 2026

[#rebooking](https://lutily.com/blog/tag/rebooking)[#client-retention](https://lutily.com/blog/tag/client-retention)[#checkout](https://lutily.com/blog/tag/checkout)

![How to Increase Salon Rebooking Rate (From 33% to 58%)](/blog/rebook-before-they-leave.webp) 

[Illustrative story.](https://lutily.com/blog/editorial) The narrator and personal experiences described are fictional.

40% Average salon rebooking rate 6 out of 10 clients leave without a next appointment

The industry average rebooking rate sits around **40%**. That means six out of ten clients walk out your door without a next appointment on the books. I know because my salon was one of them.

Two years ago I pulled my numbers and found my rebook rate was **33%**. I was spending money on Instagram ads and running promotions to bring in new clients while the ones I already had were drifting away on no particular schedule. A [Boulevard industry report](https://www.joinblvd.com/blog/salon-trends-industry-statistics) confirmed what I was seeing: most salons lose about **30% of their client base every year** just from natural attrition. That’s a hole you have to keep filling. Or you can shrink the hole.

Here’s what I changed, what worked, and the numbers behind it.

## Why rebooking matters more than new clients

Acquiring a new client costs [five to twenty-five times more](https://www.zenoti.com/thecheckin/a-guide-to-salon-client-retention-8-essential-strategies) than keeping one you already have. And a returning client spends about **31% more per visit** than a first-timer, according to [Phorest’s retention data](https://www.phorest.com/us/blog/fully-booked-salon-client-retention/).

The math scales fast. Say your average ticket is $85. A client who visits every six weeks for three years is worth roughly **$2,210**. A client who comes once and never returns is worth $85. Every missed rebook is a potential multi-year relationship walking out the door.

And frequency compounds. [Savvy Salon Club’s analysis](https://www.savvysalon.club/blog/salon-rebooking-profitability) found that tightening the average gap between visits from nine weeks to seven weeks produces a **29% increase in annual visits per client**, without adding a single new person to your book.

## The second appointment is the tipping point

Boulevard’s [Client Retention Report](https://www.salontoday.com/1088748/boulevard-report-reveals-top-performing-salons-retain-56-more-first-time-visitor) found that the second appointment is the critical conversion point. Top-performing salons convert **70%** of first visits into a second appointment and **57%** into a third. Average salons? **45%** and **39%**.

Once someone books that second visit, they’re dramatically more likely to become a regular. The journey [from first visit to loyal regular](https://lutily.com/blog/first-visit-to-regular) is where most salons lose clients, and rebooking is the bridge. And regulars are the engine. [Kitomba’s industry data](https://www.kitomba.com/blog/industry-insights-the-truth-about-regulars-and-what-they-really-mean-to-the-hair-and-beauty-industry/) shows regular clients make up about **40% of the typical client base** but account for **70% of all appointments**. A small group of loyal clients runs the whole business.

The better question: how do I make sure the clients I already have keep coming back?

## What I changed at checkout

For the first three years I owned my salon, rebooking was something the front desk handled. Clients would finish their service, walk to the register, pay, and the receptionist would say “Would you like to book your next appointment?” Most people said “I’ll check my schedule and call.” They didn’t call.

Here’s what I do now.

**The stylist starts the conversation, not the receptionist.** This was the single biggest change. While I’m still finishing up, brushing off the cape, showing them the back, I say something like “This is going to look great for about six weeks. Want me to get you on the calendar for early March?” It’s casual. It’s specific. And it comes from the person they just spent an hour with, not a stranger at a desk. A good [consultation at the start of the visit](https://lutily.com/blog/salon-consultation-first-visit) makes this moment feel natural rather than transactional.

[SalonIQ’s rebooking research](https://www.saloniq.com/article/increase-your-salon-bookings/) confirms this: when the stylist initiates the rebook instead of the front desk, conversion rates climb significantly, because the trust relationship is already built.

**I give a specific timeframe, not an open question.** “When would you like to come back?” puts the burden on the client to figure out their hair timeline. “Six weeks from now puts you at March 14th, want a Friday morning?” gives them something to say yes to.

**I frame it around their hair, not my schedule.** “Your color will start showing roots around week five” is a reason to come back. “We have openings next month” is not.

## Online booking changes the numbers

One of the most striking findings in Boulevard’s report: clients who book their first appointment **online** return for a second visit **78% of the time**. Walk-ins return at just **39%**. That’s a 2x difference. Understanding [how to handle walk-ins](https://lutily.com/blog/managing-walk-ins) and convert them into booked clients is key to closing that gap.

And clients who request a specific stylist when booking online spend **30% more per visit** than clients who don’t request anyone.

I added online booking about 18 months ago. The impact was immediate. Clients who found us through Google and booked online were already more committed before they walked in. They’d picked a stylist, chosen a time, entered their credit card. By the time they sat down, the relationship had started.

Client retention by booking method

Online — 2nd visit

78%

Walk-in — 2nd visit

39%

Online — 3rd visit

54%

Walk-in — 3rd visit

25%

_Source: [Boulevard Client Retention Report](https://www.salontoday.com/1088748/boulevard-report-reveals-top-performing-salons-retain-56-more-first-time-visitor)_

If you’re still relying on phone calls and walk-ins for new clients, online booking is the fastest lever you can pull for retention.
